My prediction: one row is one review.

My answer: 292,680 rows and 12 columns. One row is one review of one beer by one reviewer, not one beer: there are 50,826 distinct beers, 5,841 breweries, and 13,030 reviewers. So “reviews by style” counts a beer once per review; a style with a few heavily reviewed beers can look bigger than a style with many lightly reviewed ones.

Explain it back: fread() (from data.table) reads a CSV like read.csv() but is many times faster on large files, and returns a data.table.

My answer:

  • The five review_ columns are text like "14/20": the score and its scale glued together. R cannot average text.
  • beer_ABV is text too, because 14,140 rows contain "-". It means missing, not zero: real non-alcoholic beers appear in the data with ABV 0.0–0.5, and treating 14,140 missing values as zero would pull the mean ABV from 6.6 down to about 6.3 and put 14,000 beers in the “alcohol-free” bin.
  • review_time is a Unix timestamp: seconds since January 1, 1970. 1157587200 is September 7, 2006.
  • beer_style includes sake (12 styles starting with Sak), cider, perry, and mead. Several names are garbled by encoding: Klsch (Kölsch), Oktoberfest/Mrzen (Märzen), Bire de Garde, and HTML entities such as &#40;IPA&#41; for “(IPA)”. Cosmetic, but a reminder that the data went through a scraper.

Explain it back: a number column stores quantities R can add and average; a text column stores characters. "14/20" is a string of five characters, so mean() has nothing to compute until we extract the 14.

Task 3: clean it

rating_cols <- c("review_overall", "review_aroma", "review_appearance",
                 "review_palate", "review_taste")
for (col in rating_cols) beer[, (col) := as.numeric(sub("/.*", "", get(col)))]
beer[, beer_ABV := as.numeric(ifelse(beer_ABV == "-", NA, beer_ABV))]
beer[, review_date := as.Date(as.POSIXct(review_time, origin = "1970-01-01", tz = "UTC"))]
n_before <- nrow(beer)
beer <- beer[!grepl("Sak|Cider|Perry|Mead", beer_style)]
n_before - nrow(beer); nrow(beer)
## [1] 3693
## [1] 288987
summary(beer[, c(rating_cols, "beer_ABV", "review_date"), with = FALSE])

##  1st Qu.:12.0   1st Qu.: 6.000   1st Qu.:3.000     1st Qu.:3.000

##  3rd Qu.:15.0   3rd Qu.: 7.000   3rd Qu.:4.000     3rd Qu.:4.000

##  Min.   : 1.000   Min.   : 0.010   Min.   :2000-04-26  
##  1st Qu.: 6.000   1st Qu.: 5.000   1st Qu.:2006-05-18

##  3rd Qu.: 8.000   3rd Qu.: 8.000   3rd Qu.:2010-05-06  
##  Max.   :10.000   Max.   :57.700   Max.   :2012-01-13  
##                   NAs    :14019
sum(is.na(beer$beer_ABV))
## [1] 14019

My answer: overall is on a 1–20 scale, taste and aroma 1–10, appearance and palate 1–5, so a taste of 7 is 70% of its scale while an overall of 14 is 70% of a different one; they can only be compared after rescaling. Removing non-beers dropped 3,693 rows, leaving 288,987. 14,019 reviews have a missing ABV: keep them for everything about ratings, and drop them only in the ABV charts (that is what na.rm = TRUE does). Reviews run from April 2000 to January 13, 2012.

Explain it back: sub("/.*", "", x) deletes the slash and everything after it, turning "14/20" into "14"; as.numeric() then makes it a number.

Task 4: variation warm-up

style_n <- beer[, .N, by = beer_style][order(-N)][1:20]
ggplot(style_n, aes(x = reorder(beer_style, N), y = N)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) +
  labs(title = "Reviews by Style (top 20)", x = NULL, y = "Reviews") +
  theme_minimal()

ggplot(beer[!is.na(beer_ABV)], aes(beer_ABV)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5, fill = "steelblue", color = "grey20") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of ABV", x = "ABV (%)", y = "Reviews") +
  theme_minimal()

beer[which.max(beer_ABV), .(beer_name, beer_style, beer_ABV)]
##                                          beer_name beer_style beer_ABV
##                                             <char>     <char>    <num>
## 1: Schorschbru Schorschbock 57% finis coronat opus    Eisbock     57.7

My prediction: IPA most reviewed; typical ABV around 5–6%.

My answer: IPAs lead (18,635 reviews), then Pale Lager, Belgian Strong Ale, and Imperial Stout. “Most reviewed” measures what RateBeer’s users, who are enthusiasts, like to write about: Pale Lager is by far the most consumed style in the world and it is second here only because everybody has tried one. For a craft brewery, review volume is a proxy for enthusiast attention, not sales. ABV is right-skewed: most reviews are of beers between 4% and 8%, with a long tail. The maximum, Schorschbräu Schorschbock at 57.7%, is a real product (a freeze-distilled Eisbock that held the world record), not a typo. Outliers are not necessarily errors; check before dropping.

Explain it back: reorder(beer_style, N) sorts the style labels by their review count, so the bars come out in order instead of alphabetically.

Task 5: rating by style

style_stats <- beer[, .(avg = mean(review_overall), se = sd(review_overall) / sqrt(.N),
                        n = .N, abv = mean(beer_ABV, na.rm = TRUE)), by = beer_style][n >= 500]
ggplot(style_stats, aes(x = reorder(beer_style, avg), y = avg)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = avg - 1.96 * se, ymax = avg + 1.96 * se), width = 0.3) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Average Overall Rating by Style (styles with 500+ reviews)",
       x = NULL, y = "Average overall rating (out of 20)") +
  theme_minimal()

style_stats[order(-avg)][c(1:3, (.N - 2):.N), .(beer_style, avg = round(avg, 2), n, abv = round(abv, 1))]
##             beer_style   avg     n   abv
##                 <char> <num> <int> <num>
## 1:      Imperial Stout 15.85 12157  10.2
## 2:       Abt/Quadrupel 15.65  1966  10.4
## 3: Imperial/Double IPA 15.44 10559   9.1
## 4:          Pale Lager  7.45 14754   4.7
## 5:         Malt Liquor  6.77  1489   7.2
## 6:         Low Alcohol  6.37  1264   1.2

My prediction: IPAs highest, light lagers lowest.

My answer: Imperial Stout (15.9), Abt/Quadrupel (15.7), and Imperial/Double IPA (15.4) top the list; Pale Lager (7.4), Malt Liquor (6.8), and Low Alcohol (6.4) are at the bottom, less than half the top scores. The minimum-review rule keeps a style with 12 lucky reviews from topping the chart; with thousands of reviews per style the error bars are tiny, so these differences are not noise. The top styles are all strong (9–11% ABV), dark or intense; the bottom styles are light lagers around 5% or weaker. Style and alcohol content are confounded, which is exactly the next task.

Explain it back: the standard error, sd / sqrt(n), says how much the average would move if we drew another sample of reviews; mean ± 1.96 × SE is the range (95% confidence interval) where the true average plausibly sits.

Task 6: rating vs. alcohol

ggplot(beer[!is.na(beer_ABV)], aes(beer_ABV, review_overall)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.02, size = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "Overall Rating vs. ABV (all reviews)", x = "ABV (%)", y = "Overall rating") +
  theme_minimal()

abv_bins <- beer[!is.na(beer_ABV) & beer_ABV <= 15,
                 .(avg = mean(review_overall), n = .N), by = .(abv = round(beer_ABV))]
ggplot(abv_bins, aes(abv, avg)) +
  geom_line(color = "grey50") +
  geom_point(aes(size = n), color = "steelblue") +
  scale_size_continuous(labels = comma) +
  labs(title = "Average Overall Rating by ABV", x = "ABV (%, rounded)",
       y = "Average overall rating", size = "Reviews") +
  theme_minimal()

cor(beer$beer_ABV, beer$review_overall, use = "complete.obs")
## [1] 0.3985461

My prediction: stronger beers rated higher.

My answer: The raw scatter is a blob: 275,000 points on a grid of integer ratings, so nothing is visible even with transparency. Averaging within each ABV value shows a strong positive relationship: from about 11/20 at 3–4% to 15/20 at 9–10%, with a correlation of 0.40. Above 10% the curve flattens; beyond 13% the averages bounce around because few beers exist there. Causal? Not necessarily: strong beers are mostly imperial stouts, quadrupels, and barley wines, brewed with more ingredients and care, and reviewed by enthusiasts who sought them out. A 12% beer is rarely a casual purchase, so its reviews come from people predisposed to like it.

Explain it back: by = .(abv = round(beer_ABV)) groups every review by its ABV rounded to the nearest percent and averages the ratings inside each group, turning 275,000 points into 16, which is why the chart became readable.

Task 7: the brewery table

brewer <- beer[, .(n_styles = uniqueN(beer_style), n_reviews = .N,
                   avg = mean(review_overall)), by = beer_brewerId][n_reviews >= 10]
nrow(brewer); summary(brewer$n_styles)
## [1] 2439
##    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
##    1.00    5.00    8.00   10.53   13.00   49.00
ggplot(brewer, aes(n_styles, avg)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "firebrick") +
  labs(title = "Breweries: Number of Styles vs. Average Rating (10+ reviews)",
       x = "Distinct styles", y = "Average overall rating") +
  theme_minimal()

cor(brewer$n_styles, brewer$avg)
## [1] 0.3499834
brewer[order(-avg)][1]; brewer[order(avg)][1]
##    beer_brewerId n_styles n_reviews      avg
##            <int>    <int>     <int>    <num>
## 1:           623        3       422 17.36493
##    beer_brewerId n_styles n_reviews   avg
##            <int>    <int>     <int> <num>
## 1:          4603        4        48   5.5

My prediction: more styles, higher rating.

My answer: 2,439 breweries with at least 10 reviews; the median brewery has 8 styles, a quarter have 13 or more. Breadth and rating are positively related (correlation 0.35): breweries with 20+ styles average about 13.7 versus 10.6 for single-style breweries. Two stories other than “variety makes you good”: survivorship (only breweries that were already good and popular lasted long enough to launch many styles), and reverse causality (good ratings bring demand, and demand funds new styles). Highest-rated brewery with 10+ reviews: id 623 (17.4 on 422 reviews); lowest: id 4603 (5.5 on 48).

Explain it back: by = beer_brewerId collapses the 289,000 review rows into one row per brewery, computing the three summaries inside each group; the individual reviews are gone from this table, only their summaries remain.

Task 8: over time

by_year <- beer[, .(reviews = .N, avg = mean(review_overall)), by = .(year = year(review_date))][order(year)]
ggplot(by_year, aes(year, reviews)) + geom_line() + geom_point() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2000:2012) +
  labs(title = "Reviews per Year", x = NULL, y = "Reviews") + theme_minimal()

ggplot(by_year, aes(year, avg)) + geom_line() + geom_point() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2000:2012) +
  labs(title = "Average Overall Rating per Year", x = NULL, y = "Average overall rating") +
  theme_minimal()

range(beer$review_date)
## [1] "2000-04-26" "2012-01-13"

My prediction: ratings flat.

My answer: Reviews grow from 461 in 2000 to 45,112 in 2011, then “collapse” to 1,355 in 2012, because the data ends on January 13, 2012: the last year has 13 days, not a crisis. Reporting a partial period as a drop is the most common trend-chart mistake. The average rating drifts up from 12.3 (2001) to 13.5 (2011). Two non-beer explanations: the reviewer population changed (early users were hardcore critics, later ones more generous), and the mix of beers changed (the craft boom means more imperial stouts and IPAs, which score higher, in the later years).

Explain it back: year(review_date) extracts the four-digit year from a date, so by = year groups all reviews posted in the same calendar year.

Task 9: the recommendation

share <- beer[year(review_date) %in% 2002:2011,
              .(share = mean(beer_style %in% c("India Pale Ale &#40;IPA&#41;", "Imperial/Double IPA"))),
              by = .(year = year(review_date))][order(year)]
ggplot(share, aes(year, share)) + geom_line() + geom_point() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2002:2011) +
  labs(title = "Share of Reviews Going to IPAs and Double IPAs", x = NULL, y = "Share of reviews") +
  theme_minimal()

  1. Lead with a strong, intense style. Imperial stouts, quadrupels, and double IPAs average 15.4–15.9/20 versus 7.4 for pale lager (Task 5), and ratings rise with ABV up to about 10% (Task 6). A flagship in the 8–10% range plays where enthusiasts are most generous.
  2. Include an IPA and plan to grow the range. IPAs are the most reviewed style (Task 4) and their share of all reviews grew from under 5% in 2002 to 13% in 2011 (chart above); breweries with broader portfolios are rated higher (Task 7, correlation 0.35), though partly because good breweries survive to grow.
  3. Limitation: this is enthusiast attention, not sales. RateBeer users under-represent the pale-lager drinker who accounts for most beer volume, and the data has no prices, costs, or volumes. Use it to pick what wins with the enthusiast segment, and validate volume and margin elsewhere.
